config.label: One direct prompt, same model, same source, same target output

steps.rendered_prompt:
You are writing a short explainer script from a research record.

Audience: School governors and parents
Target spoken duration: about 60 seconds.

Write the script from the research record below. Make it accurate and easy to follow.

Return ONLY a JSON object, with no prose before or after it, in exactly this shape:

{
  "case_id": "C03",
  "audience": "School governors and parents",
  "target_duration_s": 60,
  "beats": [
    {"beat": "short label", "narration": "what the narrator says",
     "on_screen": "what is shown", "claim_refs": []}
  ]
}

RESEARCH RECORD
---------------
Classroom air filtration and pupil absence

Record
SYN-C03

Study design
Cluster-allocated, unblinded before-after study

Background
Respiratory illness is the largest single driver of pupil absence in primary schools in this authority, accounting for roughly half of coded absence days over the winter period. Portable high-efficiency particulate air (HEPA) cleaners reduce airborne particle counts in classroom-scale rooms, and several authorities have begun procuring them without an evaluation of absence outcomes. This study reports the first such evaluation in the authority.

Abstract
We evaluated whether portable HEPA air cleaners reduce pupil absence attributed to respiratory illness. Twenty-two primary-school classrooms in one local authority received two portable HEPA units each; eighteen classrooms in the same authority continued without units. Absence attributed to respiratory illness fell from 4.9% to 3.6% of pupil-days in intervention classrooms and from 4.7% to 4.4% in comparison classrooms over an 11-week winter term, a difference-in-differences of -1.0 percentage points (95% CI -1.9 to -0.1).

Methods
Classrooms were assigned by school leadership according to available floor space. Absence was extracted from school management-information systems using the existing respiratory-illness code, entered by school office staff during the term. Units were visible in the classrooms and were run during school hours at manufacturer setting 2. Classroom CO2 was logged. Data cover one term in one local authority. Pupil-days were counted from the school register. The difference-in-differences estimate uses classroom-level clustering with robust standard errors. CO2 loggers recorded at 5-minute intervals during occupied hours. No pupil-level data were extracted.

Statistical analysis
Statistical analysis: the primary estimate is a classroom-level difference-in-differences with robust standard errors clustered by school. Pre-period was the equivalent 11-week term of the previous academic year. Sensitivity analyses excluding the two classrooms with incomplete CO2 logs did not change the estimate materially. Absence coded for reasons other than respiratory illness was examined as a negative-control outcome and fell by 0.2 percentage points in both arms.

Results
  arm: Intervention (22 classrooms); pre: 4.9%; post: 3.6%
  arm: Comparison (18 classrooms); pre: 4.7%; post: 4.4%
  arm: Difference-in-differences; pre: -; post: -1.0 pp (95% CI -1.9 to -0.1)

Discussion
Air cleaning is an attractive intervention because it requires no behaviour change from pupils or staff. The effect size we observe, roughly one percentage point of pupil-days, is of a magnitude that would be operationally meaningful across a large authority. Schools considering procurement will want to weigh unit and running costs against the observed reduction. Wider deployment merits evaluation.

Limitations
  No laboratory confirmation of infection; the outcome is a school administrative code.
  Baseline ventilation differed between arms.

Conclusion
Portable HEPA units were associated with a reduction in coded respiratory absence of about one percentage point over a winter term.

Data availability
Classroom-level aggregate counts are available; pupil-level records are not released.

final_narration:
Respiratory illness is the biggest single cause of pupil absence in our primary schools, accounting for around half of all coded absence days across the winter.
Twenty-two classrooms in one local authority were each given two portable HEPA air cleaners. Eighteen other classrooms in the same authority carried on as normal. Absence was compared over an eleven-week winter term against the same term the year before.
In classrooms with the units, respiratory absence fell from four point nine to three point six percent of pupil-days. In classrooms without, it fell from four point seven to four point four. That is a difference of about one percentage point, though the range of uncertainty runs from nearly two points down to almost nothing.
Some caution is needed. Classrooms were not chosen at random, but by available floor space, and ventilation already differed between the two groups. Staff could see the units. And absence came from the school's own respiratory code, not from any confirmed diagnosis.
So this is an encouraging signal, not proof, from a single term in a single authority. If your school is considering air cleaners, weigh the purchase and running costs against a reduction of roughly this size, and treat any wider rollout as something still worth evaluating.
